title: Chapter 18
paragraphs: "Now there's something else I want to talk about, and you know what it is. About Anna," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, after a brief pause, shaking off the unpleasant memory.
The moment Oblonsky said Anna's name, Alexey Alexandrovitch's face changed completely; all the life went out of it, and it looked weary and dead.
"What exactly do you want from me?" he said, shifting in his chair and snapping his pince-nez shut.

"A definite settlement, Alexey Alexandrovitch — some kind of settlement of the situation. I'm appealing to you" ("not as an injured husband," Stepan Arkadyevitch was about to say, but afraid of wrecking his case with that, he changed it) "not as a statesman" (which didn't quite fit, _à propos_), "but simply as a man, and a good-hearted man and a Christian. You must take pity on her," he said.
"Meaning what, precisely?" Karenin said softly.
"Pity, yes. If you had seen her, as I have — I've been spending all winter with her — you would pity her. Her position is dreadful, just dreadful!"
"I had imagined," answered Alexey Alexandrovitch, his voice rising almost to a shrill pitch, "that Anna Arkadyevna had everything she wanted for herself."
"Oh, Alexey Alexandrovitch — for heaven's sake, let's not start trading reproaches! What's past is past, and you know what she wants and is waiting for — a divorce."

"But I believe Anna Arkadyevna refuses a divorce if I make it a condition that she leave me my son. I answered her on that basis, and I assumed the matter was closed. I consider it closed," Alexey Alexandrovitch said sharply.

"For heaven's sake, don't get heated!" Stepan Arkadyevitch said, touching his brother-in-law's knee. "The matter is not closed. Let me lay it out again. When you parted, you were as generous as anyone could possibly have been; you were ready to give her everything — freedom, even a divorce. She felt that. No, don't doubt it — she did feel it, to such a degree that in the first moment, conscious of how she had wronged you, she didn't and couldn't take everything into account. She gave it all up. But experience, and time, have shown that her position is unbearable, impossible."
"Anna Arkadyevna's life can be of no interest to me," Alexey Alexandrovitch put in, raising his eyebrows.

"Allow me not to believe that," Stepan Arkadyevitch answered gently. "Her position is intolerable for her, and benefits no one. She'll say she deserves it — you'll say so. She knows that, and she's asking nothing of you; she says plainly that she dare not ask. But I — all of us, her relatives, everyone who loves her — we are begging you, imploring you. Why must she suffer? Who is any better off for it?"
"Excuse me, but you seem to be putting me in the position of the guilty party," observed Alexey Alexandrovitch.

"Oh, no — oh, no, not at all! Please understand me," said Stepan Arkadyevitch, touching his hand again, as though sure that this physical contact would soften his brother-in-law. "All I'm saying is this: her situation is intolerable, you have the power to ease it, and you lose nothing by it. I'll arrange everything for you, so that you don't notice it. You did promise it, you know."

"The promise was given before. And I had supposed the question of my son had settled the matter. Besides, I had hoped Anna Arkadyevna had enough generosity...." Alexey Alexandrovitch got the words out with difficulty, his lips twitching and his face pale.

"She leaves it all to your generosity. She begs, she implores one thing of you — to free her from the impossible position she is in. She is not asking for her son now. Alexey Alexandrovitch, you are a good man. Put yourself in her place for a minute. The question of divorce, for her, in her position, is a matter of life and death. If you had never promised it, she would have made her peace with her position, she would have stayed living in the country. But you promised it, and she wrote to you, and she moved to Moscow. And here she's been for six months in Moscow, every chance encounter cutting her to the quick, every day waiting for an answer. It's like keeping a condemned criminal six months with the rope around his neck, promising him either death or mercy. Have pity on her, and I will undertake to arrange everything. _Vos scrupules_...."
"I'm not talking about that, not that...." Alexey Alexandrovitch broke in with disgust. "But perhaps I promised what I had no right to promise."
"So you're taking back your promise?"
"I have never refused to do what is possible, but I want time to consider how much of what I promised is possible."
"No, Alexey Alexandrovitch!" Oblonsky cried, jumping up. "I won't believe that! She's as unhappy as only an unhappy woman can be, and you cannot refuse in such...."
"As much of what I promised as is possible. _Vous professez d'être libre penseur._ But as a believer I cannot, in a matter of such gravity, act in violation of the Christian law."
"But in Christian societies, and in ours so far as I know, divorce is permitted," said Stepan Arkadyevitch. "Divorce is sanctioned by our church, even. And we see...."
"It's allowed, but not in the sense...."

"Alexey Alexandrovitch, you don't sound like yourself," Oblonsky said after a brief pause. "Wasn't it you (and didn't all of us admire you for it?) who forgave everything, and, moved purely by Christian feeling, was ready to make any sacrifice? You said yourself: if a man takes thy coat, give him thy cloak also — and now...."
"I beg you," Alexey Alexandrovitch said shrilly, suddenly springing to his feet, his face white, his jaw twitching, "I beg you to drop this — to drop this subject!"

"Oh, no — oh, forgive me, forgive me if I've hurt you," Stepan Arkadyevitch said, holding out his hand with an embarrassed smile. "I'm only the messenger; I was simply delivering the message that had been given to me."
Alexey Alexandrovitch gave him his hand, thought for a moment, and said:
"I must think it over and seek guidance. The day after tomorrow I'll give you a final answer," he said, after another moment of thought.
